| Error card                                            | Class, message, stack trace, and [the source code around the failing line](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#errors-with-source-code) |
| Waterfall                                             | Every span this request ran, as a timeline                                                                                          |
| Logs                                                  | The lines this request wrote, on the same clock as the waterfall                                                                    |
| Spans table                                           | The same spans ranked by [self time](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#self-time-vs-total-time)                                       |

From the header you can also create an [alert rule](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md) or an [issue](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md) already scoped to this operation, and - when the request failed or ran unusually slowly - [copy the whole page as a prompt for a coding agent](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#hand-it-to-a-coding-agent).

> [!INFO] The same data is queryable live by an MCP-connected agent - `list_slow_operations`, then `get_operation_details` for a specific route and the trace ids behind it. See [MCP server](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/mcp.md).

### Is this call actually slow?

A duration on its own means nothing: 400ms is alarming for a cache read and excellent for a report. So the request and job detail pages compare the execution against other calls of the _same_ operation, in the same window and application, and state a verdict:

- **Faster than average**
- **Typical** - slower than the mean, which is true of roughly half of all calls. Not a problem.
- **Slower than 95% of calls** - past p95. This one is genuinely unusual.

![Request duration](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/request-duration.webp)

The comparison needs a real sample to be worth anything. Below 20 comparable calls in the selected window, the page widens the baseline to the last day and says which window the numbers came from; with fewer than two calls the card doesn't render at all rather than let a call measure itself. Search terms are deliberately excluded from the baseline's scope - a baseline filtered by whatever you typed into a search box is not a baseline.

### Was the process to blame?

Knowing an operation is slow doesn't say _why_. Often the code didn't change at all and the process underneath it did: the event loop fell behind, the box ran out of CPU, garbage collection started eating the window. The **Under host pressure** card on an operation's page answers that directly, by splitting the operation's own calls in two and comparing them:

> [!INFO] When event loop delay is elevated (> 37.2 ms), this operation's p95 is **1.8× slower** - 24% of calls landed in those buckets.

![Under host pressure](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/under-host-pressure.webp)

Underneath the sentence are both sides of the split - p95, average, and call count when the host was normal, and the same three when it was under pressure - so you can see the size of the effect rather than take the ratio on faith. If more than one metric qualifies, the strongest leads and the rest follow as chips.

Four host metrics are tested, all of them the same series the [Profiler](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/profiler.md) charts:

| Metric               | What an elevated reading means for this operation                                         |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Event loop delay** | Calls waited before their callbacks even started - the classic "fast spans, slow request" |
| **CPU usage**        | The process was competing for CPU, so every phase of the call stretched                   |
| **Memory usage**     | Heap pressure, usually alongside the GC row rather than instead of it                     |
| **GC time**          | Wall-clock time the collector took while these calls were in flight                       |

**"Elevated" means the metric's own top quartile in the window you're looking at**, not a fixed threshold: the point of comparison is this process against itself, and a CPU number that's alarming for one service is idle for the next. The card prints the cutoff it used so the claim can be checked.

Two things this card deliberately does not do. It doesn't chart a single execution against host metrics - runtime metrics are bucketed, and one 90ms request cannot resolve against a 60-second bucket, so an overlay would look explanatory while saying nothing. And it doesn't claim causation: the host and the operation moved together, which is evidence, not proof. A batch job hammering the same process is just as good an explanation as the operation being the victim - which is why the next step is [the Profiler for the same window](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/profiler.md#working-with-the-rest-of-the-dashboard).

The card is absent far more often than it's present, and that's the design. It renders only when all of the following hold, and stays silent otherwise rather than dressing up noise as a finding:

- The metric actually moved during the window. A host that was flat has no "elevated" state to compare against.
- Both sides of the split hold at least 20 calls, so the comparison is between distributions rather than anecdotes.
- The elevated side is at least 1.5× slower. Below that, the difference is within the noise of the sample.

If you expected the card and don't see it, widen the time range: more buckets give the split more traffic and the host more room to have varied. An operation whose latency genuinely doesn't track the host will never show it, which is itself an answer - it points the investigation back at the code, the database, or whatever the spans are waiting on.

## Services

Endpoints tell you _what_ is slow. **Services** tells you _which class_ makes it so - a per-application view over your NestJS classes, in the vocabulary you wrote the code in rather than a list of routes.

![Services](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/services.webp)

Every row is a class your SDK instrumented, with:

- **Own time** - time spent in the class's _own_ code, with everything its methods awaited subtracted out. This is the number that answers "where is the time actually going," shown with its **share** of all self time in the window, and it's what the table sorts by default.
- **Total time** - wall time of calls passing _through_ the class, nested work included. Deliberately shown smaller and muted, because leading with it produces a wrong answer by default.

A controller that awaits a service that awaits a repository has a large total and a self time near zero - it did no work of its own. Sort by total and that controller tops the list for doing nothing; sort by self (the default) and the repository actually burning the time surfaces instead. This is the same self-vs-total distinction spans use in the trace waterfall - see [Self time vs. total time](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#self-time-vs-total-time) - one level up: per class instead of per span.

Expand a row to drill into that class's methods, with the same own/total split per method. Calls, errors, and method count round out the row; sorting by own time, total time, or calls all query the server directly, so the ranking holds even past the first page.

Two things worth knowing about the numbers themselves:

- **Drivers are not classes.** The agent files a database query under its driver (`pg`, `mysql2`, `mssql`, `mongodb`) and an outbound call under `http`. Those are not classes you wrote, so they are not listed here; the time a repository spent waiting on its query counts as that repository's own time, the same rule the [spans table](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md) applies.
- **Only instrumented classes appear.** Attribution comes from the SDK's own instrumentation - a class it doesn't wrap contributes nothing, no matter how much traffic it handles. A short or empty list almost always means low instrumentation coverage, not low traffic, and the page says so rather than showing "No data."
- **Under span sampling, absolute numbers are a sample.** A project with [span sampling](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#spend-controls) enabled only sees the sampled traces reflected here, so raw millisecond totals should be read as indicative. Relative ordering and each class's _share_ stay meaningful regardless - which is why they're what the page leads with.

## Errors

**Errors** mirrors Requests but for failures - every error that escaped a request handler, `NotFoundException`s and other 4xx exceptions included, grouped by operation, with the same drill-down into individual occurrences. The first time a project reports an unhandled error it has never seen before, its members are emailed about it - on every plan; see [the built-in new-error email](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md#the-built-in-new-error-email).

![Errors](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/errors.webp)

An individual error _is_ the failed request, so the error detail page is the request detail page with the failure leading instead of buried under the details grid: error class, message, stack trace, and source code first, then the request's own context, then the waterfall and logs. Error monitoring is included on every plan with no extra setup - the SDK captures it automatically.

### Grouping errors into defects

A spike of 3,140 `TypeError`s is one bug, not 3,140 of them. The **Group into defects** switch on the Errors page reads the same failures as defects instead of occurrences: the same exception class and the same normalized stack shape collapse into one **error group**, fingerprinted server-side, regardless of how the message was worded, which line numbers moved, or which deploy produced it.

![Defects](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/defects.webp)

A group carries what triage needs rather than what a single occurrence has:

| Field                    | What it tells you                                                       |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Class and sample message | What the defect is, taken from its first occurrence                     |
| Status                   | Open, Resolved, or Ignored                                              |
| First and last seen      | Whether it's new, ongoing, or has gone away                             |
| Introduced in            | The release the first occurrence ran on, when it reported one           |
| Occurrences              | How often it fired **in the selected window**, not all time             |
| Issue                    | The [issue](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md) it was promoted to, if any |

The two closed states are deliberately not symmetric. **Resolved** is a claim about the code, so the server reopens the group the moment the bug recurs - a fix that didn't hold surfaces itself instead of staying quietly green. **Ignored** is a decision about the noise, and stays ignored.

From a group you can open its detail drawer and promote it into an issue in one click. Promoting a group that already has an open issue links to that issue rather than opening a second one; promoting again after the issue was resolved or closed starts a fresh one.

![Defect individual](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/defect-individual.webp)

> [!INFO] Grouping starts from when fingerprinting was deployed. Errors ingested before that carry no fingerprint and aren't counted in a group, so a group's history can be shorter than your retention window.

The switch is a reading of the page, not a different page: occurrences are still there for chasing a spike in the moment, and the view you picked travels in the URL, so a grouped view is linkable.

## Jobs

**Jobs** covers background work - queue consumers, cron runs, anything outside the request/response cycle - with the same three levels as Requests, and the same tracing, alerting, and agent-prompt treatment. A slow consumer is exactly as visible as a slow endpoint.

![Jobs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/jobs.webp)

A job run carries a few fields a request doesn't:

- **Queue wait** - how long the job sat between being enqueued and being picked up. A job that "takes 30 seconds" is a very different problem depending on whether 29 of them were spent waiting for a free worker.
- **Attempts** - which try this was, for jobs your queue retries.
- **Status** and **failure reason** - how the run ended, and the reason the queue recorded for it.
- **Job ID** and **queue name** - for finding the same run in your queue's own tooling.

> [!INFO] Or ask an MCP-connected agent - see `list_jobs` and `get_job_details` in [MCP server](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/mcp.md).

A job's detail page charts queue wait (average and p95) alongside throughput and processing time, so you can watch a backlog grow rather than only finding out once it's already burned through - see [queue wait alerts](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md#queue-wait-alerts) to be notified while it's still growing.

## Spans

**Spans** is the analytics view over the **custom spans** your code creates with [`TracerService.createSpan()`](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#creating-spans) - the same way Requests is the analytics view over requests. Use it to answer questions that cut across routes: "how slow is `OrdersService.recalculate` everywhere it's called", rather than "how slow is this one endpoint".

> [!INFO] Auto-instrumented spans are not listed here. Every request records a full span tree - controller and service calls, database queries, outbound HTTP - and each controller and service span is its own [Observability Event](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#usage), counted under **Spans** on the Usage page. Query and outbound HTTP spans [aren't billed](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#database-queries-and-outbound-http). You read them in the [trace waterfall](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#reading-the-waterfall) of a single execution, not on this page. An application that never calls `createSpan()` will therefore show a large Spans figure in Usage alongside an empty Spans page - that is expected, not a gap in the data. To bring the figure down, use [span sampling](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#spend-controls).

![Spans](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/spans.webp)

Drilling into a single span invocation opens it _in the context of its trace_: the waterfall renders the whole trace with that span singled out, and the logs card defaults to the slice of the trace clock the span occupied. See [Traces & spans](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md).

## Traces

A **trace** is everything recorded under a single trace id - the request or job that started it, and every span underneath it. Distributed traces follow work across multiple applications in the same project: a request that fans out from your API into another HTTP or RPC service still resolves to one trace once that service is set up to propagate the trace id - see [SDK → Propagating trace ids between services](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#propagating-trace-ids-between-services). Queue jobs join in on their own: a job added from inside a traced request runs under that request's trace id, wherever its worker lives.

Every execution page links to its trace, and every trace page links back to the request or job that started it. [Traces & spans](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md) covers the waterfall, self time, error source frames, and log correlation in detail.

> [!INFO] A trace id is also all an MCP-connected agent needs - see `get_trace` and `get_trace_logs` in [MCP server](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/mcp.md).

![Trace waterfall](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/traces.webp)

## Users

**Users** shows the end users interacting with your project, when your application reports a user identifier alongside its telemetry. Beyond "who was affected", the per-user view groups a user's calls into the actions they actually performed and draws the paths between them - see [Users](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/users.md).

## Custom metrics

Beyond what's auto-instrumented, applications can report their own **counters and gauges** - anything domain-specific, like orders processed or queue depth. These show up under **Custom**, grouped by metric name and any labels you attach, with the same time-series charting as everything else, and they can be [alerted on](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md) like any built-in metric.

A counter reads as "unknown" rather than zero until its application has reported it at least once since the metric was added. That's a real state, not missing data: "we have never heard from this metric" and "this metric is currently zero" are different facts, and showing the second when you mean the first hides a broken deploy.

## Map

**Activity → Map** draws how a project's applications, queues and databases talk to each other. It always covers the whole project, and follows the time range.

![Service map](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/map.webp)

Applications and queues run left to right in call order. The databases and external services an application depends on hang beneath it. Each line carries its volume (thickness, and how fast the traffic along it moves) and its health (a soft red above a 1% error rate, the full brand red above 5% - teal means healthy). Hover anything to isolate what it touches; click it for the numbers - on a database, the statements the time went to; on an application, what it calls and what calls it, with a link to its requests.

Nothing has to be configured, because nothing new is collected:

- **Databases and external services** come from the agent's [query and outbound-HTTP spans](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#database-queries-and-outbound-http). One database node per application and driver - two services on Postgres are usually two databases, and nothing on the wire says otherwise - and one node per external host, shared by everyone who calls it (the busiest eight per application).
- **Queues** come from the jobs an application works.
- **Links between applications, and from an application to a queue,** are inferred from executions that share a [trace id](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#propagating-trace-ids-between-services) - the agent forwards it on outbound HTTP and stamps it on the jobs a request enqueues. They are drawn dashed, and measured on the most recent requests rather than the whole window, so read them as "this calls that", not as an exact count.

An application with no lines almost always runs an agent older than 0.3, which does not report queries or outbound calls.

## Releases

**Releases** compares each version of an application against the one before it - error rate, latency, and throughput side by side - so a regression introduced by a deploy is visible immediately rather than buried in a week-long chart. Every request and job also records the release that served it, so once Releases tells you _which_ version broke, the executions from that version are one filter away.

![Releases](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/sdk/deployments.webp)

### What changed in the code

Open a release and, under its error-rate breakdown, **What changed in the code** lists the queries, outbound calls and methods whose behavior moved across the boundary by more than noise:

- **New** or **Gone** - a statement, an external host or a method that only one side of the boundary called, often enough that its absence on the other side is not chance.
- **44× calls** - a statement or call made that many times more per request. A new N+1 reads exactly like this, usually long before it moves a p95.
- **7.6× slower**, **2× faster** - a method's own time per call, or a query's, compared on enough calls either side to mean something.

Each row carries its calls per request and own time per call on both sides, and the time it adds to (or takes from) an average request, which is what the list is ranked by. It reads the same windows either side of the boundary as the verdict, from the class-level telemetry the [Services](#services) page uses, so nothing extra is collected. Rates are per request of the whole application, not per route: a row names the statement, and a trace of the route shows where it runs.

## Logs

**Logs** streams everything your services logged, correlated to the traces they ran in. From a slow or failed request you can jump straight to the log lines it produced, and from a log line back to its trace.

On an execution or trace page the logs card does more than list lines:

- Each line is placed on the **trace's clock** - its offset from the start of the trace - and names the span that was in flight when it was written, so you can see what the code was doing at that moment.
- Hovering a line **marks that instant on the waterfall above**, which answers "what was running when this was logged" without counting milliseconds by hand.
- A **level floor** filters to a level and everything louder (`warn` and above, say). `fatal` is never filtered out.
- A trace returns at most 1,000 lines. When a trace logged more than that, the card says so - the absence of a line you expected is then a truncation, not evidence.

Logs streaming is available on Pro, Scale, and Enterprise; Free does not include log ingestion.

![Logs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/logs.webp)

## Profiler

**Profiler** shows runtime health per application - CPU, memory, event loop delay, garbage collection - over time, and compares instances against each other when an application runs on more than one. See [Profiler](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/profiler.md).

![Profiler](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/profiler.webp)

## A worked path through the dashboard

The views are designed to be walked in order. A typical investigation:

1. An [alert](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md) fires, or the **Requests** chart shows p95 climbing.
2. Sort the route list by duration or failure rate to find which operation moved.
3. Open the operation. Is it constant or spiky? Did it start at a deploy? Check **Releases**.
4. Open a single execution from the tail of the distribution - one the baseline card calls _slower than 95% of calls_.
5. Read the **waterfall**: which span holds the [self time](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#self-time-vs-total-time)?
6. If it failed, read the **error card** - stack trace and the source lines around the throw.
7. Check the **logs** for that trace, hovering lines to line them up with the spans.
8. [Copy the agent prompt](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#hand-it-to-a-coding-agent) and hand the whole thing to a coding agent, or open an [issue](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md) linked to the execution so whoever picks it up starts where you stopped.

The same walk is available to an agent over the [MCP server](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/mcp.md), one tool per step - `find_regressions` or `list_slow_operations` at the top, `get_trace` and `get_trace_logs` at the bottom - when you'd rather ask questions than click through them.

---

# Traces & spans

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/traces

A **trace** is everything your applications recorded under a single trace id: the request or job that started it, and every span underneath. It is the unit of diagnosis - an aggregate tells you a route got slower, a trace tells you which line of code to open.

Traces are captured automatically on every plan. You don't create them, sample them by hand, or wire the parent/child relationships yourself: the SDK's auto-instrumentation does it, and any spans you add manually slot into the same tree.

![Trace waterfall](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/traces.webp)

## Trace correlation

A trace only becomes **one** trace, instead of several disconnected ones, because every service involved in it agrees on the same trace id. Within a single service this is automatic: the SDK generates a trace id when work starts, and every span underneath - including ones you add manually - inherits it. Across services, three channels carry it on their own: outbound HTTP calls forward it as an `x-request-id` header, TCP and Redis microservice clients send it in the packet's metadata (`@nestjs/microservices` 12.0.4 and later), and a job queued from inside a traced operation takes it along to whichever worker runs it. Everything else - an API call that fans out to a gRPC service, a message over NATS, RabbitMQ, Kafka or MQTT - only shows up here as one trace if the trace id gets forwarded from caller to callee; left unconfigured, each service mints its own, and the same user action shows up as several separate traces instead of one.

Where it isn't automatic, forwarding the trace id is application code, not a dashboard setting - see [SDK → Propagating trace ids between services](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#propagating-trace-ids-between-services) for what each transport needs, including the Node version automatic HTTP forwarding depends on for axios-style clients.

The same trace id is also what correlates a trace with the logs it produced (see [Logs on the trace's clock](#logs-on-the-traces-clock) below) and with the request or job page that started it.

![Trace correlation](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/service-flow.webp)

## Spans

A **span** is one timed operation inside a trace: a controller method, a service call, a database query, an outbound HTTP request, or anything you've instrumented yourself. Each span carries:

| Field        | Meaning                                                                       |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name         | `Class.method` for auto-instrumented code, or the name you gave a custom span |
| Duration     | Wall-clock time from the span's start to its end, including its children      |
| Start offset | Where it began on the trace's clock, measured from the root                   |
| Parent       | The span that called it - what makes the trace a tree rather than a list      |
| Outcome      | Whether it completed or threw                                                 |
| Error        | Class, message, stack trace, and source frames, when it threw                 |
| Tags         | Whatever your application attached to it                                      |

Spans you name yourself - the ones created with [`TracerService.createSpan()`](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#creating-spans) - also get their own analytics view (**Spans** in the project dashboard), aggregating every invocation of a given span name across every route that calls it. That's the view for "is `OrdersService.recalculate` slow everywhere, or only from this one endpoint?" - a question the per-route views can't answer, because they group by the caller rather than by the work.

Auto-instrumented spans are deliberately left out of that view: they're recorded on every trace, they're the bulk of your span volume, and their names are framework internals nobody aggregates by. They are still fully visible - in the waterfall below, on the execution page's spans table, and in your [Usage](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#usage) totals under **Spans**.

Opening a single span invocation shows it _in the context of its trace_, not on its own: the full waterfall renders with that span singled out, and the logs card defaults to the slice of the trace's clock the span occupied. A span's duration in isolation is rarely the answer; a span's duration next to its siblings usually is.

## Reading the waterfall

The waterfall draws the span tree against time: nesting depth as indentation, duration as bar length, position as when the span ran. Everything about it is tuned for one job - finding where the time went in a real trace, which is almost always heavily skewed.

- **The scale is linear.** A log or square-root scale would make the bars easier to look at and would misstate magnitude, which is the entire point of drawing bars.
- **Insignificant subtrees open collapsed.** A subtree accounting for less than 1% of the trace starts closed, with a count of what's hidden inside it. Real traces routinely put one 34ms span next to thirty spans at 0.00ms; the view opens on the spans that hold the time, and the noise is one click away.
- **Depth is coloured on an ordinal ramp**, not with categorical hues - the colour tells you how deep you are, not which service you're in.
- **Failing spans are marked.** A span that threw carries a warning marker, so a deep failure isn't something you have to hunt for by expanding every branch.
- **Overlapping children are flagged.** When a span's children sum to more than the span's own duration, they ran concurrently - `Promise.all`, a parallel fan-out - and the row says so rather than reporting a nonsensical negative.
- **Queries and outbound calls show what they were.** A database query or an outbound HTTP request is a row of its own, under the method that made it, with an icon, the operation (`SELECT orders`, `POST api.stripe.com`) and the statement or URL running on beside it - visible without a hover. The row's caret opens the full statement, laid out by clause with its placeholders highlighted, and a copy button. Values are never there to show: the agent removes them before anything is sent.
- **Hovering a log line marks its instant on the bars.** The waterfall and the logs card share the trace's clock, so "what was running when this was logged" is a hover, not an arithmetic exercise.

![A query opened in the waterfall](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/sql.webp)

### Self time vs. total time

The single most useful number in a trace is **self time**: a span's duration minus everything its children accounted for. It is the time the span spent in _its own_ code.

Ranking by total duration is what most people try first, and it always produces the same useless answer: the controller at the top, because it contains everything. In a trace measured here, `TelemetryRecorderController.insert` reports 40.42ms total but 0.04ms self - it does nothing except call the service beneath it. Ranking by self time surfaces `TelemetryRecorderService.insertRequestsTelemetry` at 34.39ms, which is where the request actually spent its time.

So every execution page carries a spans table under the waterfall, with four columns - **Name**, **Self %**, **Self**, **Total** - sorted so the code that did the work comes first. When a span's children overlapped in time, its true self time is unknowable (the recorded durations overlap), so it is shown as 0 with a tooltip saying why, rather than as a negative number or a guess.

Between the waterfall and that table, most latency questions resolve in two reads: which span holds the self time, and what was it waiting on.

The spans table under the waterfall lists **your application's methods only**. The agent's query and outbound-HTTP spans are left out of it, and their time is read as the calling method's own: the table answers "which of my methods burned the time", and thirty rows of `SELECT order_items` would bury the repository method that ran them. The waterfall is where the individual queries are.

## How long waterfalls are kept

Spans are the bulk of what your applications report - a single request records a whole tree of them - so they're kept on a shorter clock than the executions they hang off.

**After 7 days, the span tree is dropped from executions that were both fast and successful**: under 1 second, no 5xx, and no failed job or operation. Anything that was slow _or_ failed keeps its spans for your plan's full [retention window](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md) - which is the set you actually come back to weeks later.

Only the spans go. The request or job itself stays for the full window with its duration, status, error, source context, tags, and [logs](#logs-on-the-traces-clock) intact, and every aggregate - percentiles, error rates, [SLOs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/slos.md) - is computed from those records rather than from spans, so none of them thin out over time. What you lose on an old, uneventful trace is the waterfall and the spans table beneath it.

This only bites on plans that retain more than 7 days. On Free, the 3-day window gets there first and nothing is ever pruned this way.

## Errors, with source code

When a trace contains a failure, the execution page leads with an error card rather than making you dig for it. The card resolves _one_ error - the first span that threw, walking the tree depth-first, or the trace-level error when no individual span carried one - because a page that shows six framework re-raises of the same failure buries the one that matters.

The card shows:

1. **Error class and message**, and the span it was thrown inside.
2. **The stack trace**, trimmed to what's worth reading: your application's frames first, with the throwing frame marked, and the dependency and Node-internal frames condensed underneath. Paths are rewritten relative to your project root, so a frame reads `src/orders/orders.service.ts:35` rather than `/var/app/current/dist/orders/orders.service.js:35` - the first one you can open, the second one you can't. If your frames do come out looking like the second one, your build is running without source maps - see [Source maps](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#source-maps).
3. **The source code around the failing lines.** When your build ships source context, the card renders the actual lines from your repository with the throwing statement marked, so you can see the code that failed without leaving the dashboard, switching to your editor, or checking out the release that was running. The throwing frame's source is open; each calling frame's is one click away, with the call it made marked.

That last part is what makes an error report actionable on its own: class, message, file, line, and the surrounding code, in one card, for a failure that happened in production on a build you may not have checked out.

![Error card with source context](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/error-with-source.webp)

## Logs on the trace's clock

The logs a trace produced are shown beneath its waterfall, correlated by trace id. Each line is placed at its offset from the start of the trace and labelled with the span that was in flight when it was written; hovering a line marks that instant on the waterfall above. A level floor narrows to a level and everything louder, and `fatal` is never filtered out.

A trace returns at most 1,000 lines. When a trace wrote more, the card says so - so a missing line reads as truncation rather than as evidence that the code never ran. Logs require Pro or above; see [Telemetry → Logs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#logs).

## Hand it to a coding agent

> [!INFO] Instead of using the "Copy agent prompt" button, you can also use the [MCP server](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/mcp.md) to connect an MCP-compatible agent (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, your own agent) straight to the API. The agent can then keep asking: investigate a regression, follow a trace into its logs, check whether an error is still happening - without you relaying each answer back. Scoped to exactly what you can see in the dashboard, and read-only apart from setting up a service and resolving an issue once its fix ships.

Reading a trace tells you what happened. The next step is always the same: go find that code and change it. The **Copy agent prompt** button does that handoff in one click - it copies the entire page as a self-contained markdown prompt, ready to paste into a coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, or anything else that has your repository open).

![Copy agent prompt button](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/copy-agent-prompt.webp)

### Where it appears

The button is deliberately not on every page. It shows up only where there is something to investigate:

| Page                   | Shown when                                                            | Prompt is framed as         |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Request / error detail | The request failed, or was slower than 95% of calls to the same route | An error, or a slow request |
| Job detail             | The run failed, or was slower than 95% of runs of the same job        | A failed job, or a slow job |
| Trace detail           | The trace contains an error                                           | A failing trace             |

A run that both failed _and_ dragged is framed as the failure - the error is the concrete thing to fix, and the latency usually follows from it. An ordinary successful call of ordinary duration gets no button: there is nothing to ask about, and a button that is always present stops reading as a signal.

### What gets copied

The prompt is plain markdown with no links back into the dashboard, because it's pasted into a tool that has your repository but not this app - everything it needs has to travel in the text:

- **The task.** One opening line telling the agent what kind of problem this is, so it looks for the right thing: a request that threw sends it somewhere different than a request that was merely slow.
- **Context.** Operation, status, duration, application, release, protocol, user, timestamp, trace id, and tags. For jobs, also queue wait, attempts, and failure reason.
- **The error.** Class, message, the span it was thrown in, the trimmed stack trace with the throwing frame marked and paths relative to the project root, and the source lines around each failing frame.
- **How this compares.** This call's duration against the operation's average and p95, and the size and window of the sample - so the agent knows whether it's chasing a genuine outlier or normal behaviour.
- **Where the time went.** The top spans by self time, with self, total, and share of the trace, and a note where children overlapped. Capped at 15: the tail of a long trace is sub-millisecond spans that answer nothing and cost context window.
- **The logs.** Up to 40 lines from the trace, chosen errors-and-warnings first so the cap can never drop the one line that says what went wrong, then printed back in chronological order so the sequence reads as it happened. If the trace was truncated at the 1,000-line cap, the prompt says so.
- **What to do.** Closing instructions asking the agent to locate the named code (span names are `Class.method`), explain the root cause from the code rather than from the symptom, propose a fix as a diff with tests, and - importantly - say what's missing instead of guessing when the data isn't enough.

The copy happens against your clipboard, so it needs a secure context; if the browser refuses, the button says so rather than reporting a success you didn't get.

### Why this rather than a screenshot

Pasting a stack trace into a chat window loses the parts that make the failure diagnosable: the timings, the release, the tags, the logs around it, and the fact that this call was in the slowest 5% rather than merely slow-looking. The prompt carries all of it, already trimmed to what fits usefully in a context window and already rewritten into paths that exist in your working tree. What the agent gets is what you would have written out by hand after ten minutes of copying between tabs.

## Where to go next

- [Telemetry](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md) - the views these traces hang off, and how to walk from an alert down to a single execution.
- [Users](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/users.md) - the same executions, grouped by who performed them.
- [Issues](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md) - link a trace to tracked work so the next person starts with the telemetry, not a description of it.

---

# Using the MCP server

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/mcp

The API exposes an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server, so an MCP-compatible client - Claude Code, Claude Desktop, your IDE, an agent you wrote yourself - can ask questions about your projects directly instead of you copying dashboard data into a prompt. Regressions, slow operations, error groups, traces, jobs, alerts: the same data the dashboard shows, scoped to exactly what you can see.

The endpoint speaks Streamable HTTP at `POST https://observe-api.nestjs.com/mcp`. It's stateless - there's no session to open, nothing to keep alive, and no setup beyond the request itself.

> [!INFO] MCP is one of two ways to get telemetry to an agent. [Copy agent prompt](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#hand-it-to-a-coding-agent) packages one page as text for a single paste; MCP is for an agent that needs to keep asking - follow a trace, check whether the error is still firing - without you relaying each answer.

## An example investigation

The tools are shaped around investigations rather than endpoints, so each answer carries the key the next question needs. A deploy went out and something feels wrong:

1. **"What regressed after the last deploy?"** - `find_regressions` compares error rate and latency either side of each release boundary and names the release that made things worse, along with the operations it degraded. `diff_release` then says what that release changed in the code - an N+1, a new outbound call, a slower method.
2. **"Show me that operation."** - `get_operation_details` returns the route's latency and error summary plus recent individual requests, each with a `traceId`.
3. **"What did that request actually do?"** - `get_trace` resolves the trace id into the waterfall: every execution under it, across services, with span trees.
4. **"What did the code say while it happened?"** - `get_trace_logs` returns every log line emitted under the same trace id, in order.

Errors and background jobs follow the same shape: `list_error_groups` → `get_error_details` → `get_trace`, and `list_jobs` → `get_job_details` → `get_trace`. Start with `list_projects` in any case - almost every diagnostic tool takes a `projectId`.

## Getting a token

Personal MCP tokens are minted in the dashboard under [MCP tokens](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/dashboard/mcp-tokens).

- Click **Create token**, give it a name, and optionally set an expiry. A token with no expiry never expires - MCP clients have no refresh flow.
- The secret (`omcp_...`) is shown **once**, in the response to creating it. Copy it immediately; only its hash is stored, so it cannot be retrieved again. Lost it? Revoke the token and mint another.
- Tokens act **as the user who created them**, with their exact project permissions. If you can't see something in the dashboard, neither can the token.
- MCP follows the plan that pays for each project. If your own plan includes MCP, the token reaches every project you can see. If it doesn't - say you're on Free, invited into a team on a paid plan - the token reaches only the projects whose plan includes MCP, and the others refuse with a 403.

Revoking a token from the same page cuts it off immediately. The list shows each token's name, expiry, and when it was last used, which is how you tell a token still in use from one to retire.

> [!INFO] Token management itself is dashboard-only, on purpose: an MCP token cannot mint or revoke MCP tokens, so a leaked credential can't extend its own life.

## Connecting a client

Any client that speaks Streamable HTTP can connect: there's one URL and one header, and no OAuth dance to sit through. What differs between clients is only where the config file lives and what its keys are called.

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add observe --transport http https://observe-api.nestjs.com/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"
```

### Claude Desktop, and other `mcpServers` clients

The block most clients read - Claude Desktop, and anything that copied its shape. Claude Desktop's config is at `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` on macOS, `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` on Windows:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "observe": {
      "url": "https://observe-api.nestjs.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <token>" }
    }
  }
}
```

### Cursor

The same `mcpServers` shape, in `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project or `.cursor/mcp.json` for one. Cursor expands `${env:...}` inside `url` and `headers`, which is how you keep the token out of a file you might commit:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "observe": {
      "url": "https://observe-api.nestjs.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:OBSERVE_MCP_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code (Copilot agent mode)

VS Code uses `servers` rather than `mcpServers`, wants an explicit `type`, and can prompt for the token once and store it encrypted instead of keeping it in the file. In `.vscode/mcp.json` for one workspace, or your user `mcp.json` for all of them:

```json
{
  "inputs": [
    {
      "type": "promptString",
      "id": "observe-token",
      "description": "NestJS Observe MCP token",
      "password": true
    }
  ],
  "servers": {
    "observe": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://observe-api.nestjs.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:observe-token}" }
    }
  }
}
```

### Your own agent

With the official TypeScript SDK, the endpoint is a `StreamableHTTPClientTransport` and the token rides in `requestInit.headers`:

```ts
const client = new Client({ name: "my-agent", version: "1.0.0" });

await client.connect(
  new StreamableHTTPClientTransport(
    new URL("https://observe-api.nestjs.com/mcp"),
    {
      requestInit: {
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OBSERVE_MCP_TOKEN}` },
      },
    }
  )
);

const { tools } = await client.listTools();
```

Python and the other official SDKs expose the same two knobs - a URL and request headers - under their own names.

### Checking the connection

Before debugging a client's config, confirm the endpoint and token work at all. This lists the tools the server would advertise:

```bash
curl -s https://observe-api.nestjs.com/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

A tool list back means the credential is good and anything still broken is client-side. A 401 means the token is - see [When something fails](#when-something-fails).

> [!INFO] Clients disagree about key names (`mcpServers` vs. `servers`), and some want a `type` (`"http"` or `"streamable-http"`) that others infer from the URL. If yours isn't listed, look for its remote-server syntax and fill in the same two values: the URL and an `Authorization: Bearer` header.

A dashboard session JWT also works as a bearer credential, which is handy if your client already holds one - the server can't tell the two apart once they resolve to a user. Personal MCP tokens are still the intended long-lived credential: they outlive a session, they're revocable one at a time, and they carry a name so you know which client to cut off.

## Available tools

Almost every tool only reads; the ones that write are listed under [Setting up a service](#setting-up-a-service) and [Resolving an issue](#resolving-an-issue). Descriptions below are the ones the server advertises to your client.

Every answer ends with the dashboard pages it came from, in a text block after the JSON: the page itself, and for pages that exist per row - a trace, an error class, a job - a template such as `.../traces/{traceId}` the agent fills from the row. When an agent tells you something, the chart it read that from is one click away. Links are built from the API's configured dashboard address, and the JSON before them is exactly what it was without them.

Most diagnostic tools share a scope: a required `projectId`, an optional `applicationId` to narrow to one service, and an optional `timeInterval` look-back window (`1h`, `3h`, `12h`, `1d`, `3d`, `7d`, `30d`), defaulting to `1d`.

### Navigation

| Tool                  | What it answers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_projects`       | Every project you're a member of, with team and application counts. Start here to resolve project ids.                                                                                                                                                               |
| `get_project`         | One project by id, including your access level (read/write/admin) and subscription state.                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `list_issues`         | [Issues](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md) across your projects, newest first; filterable by project, status, or limit.                                                                                                                                                         |
| `get_issue`           | One issue by id, including its comments and activity.                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `get_incident_record` | An issue's [incident record](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md#incident-record): what it was about, when it started and ended, the release it came in with, the users and customers it reached, the fix and its verification, and a timeline of those moments.                   |
| `list_slos`           | A project's [SLOs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/slos.md) with current status and error-budget burn. A burning SLO names the operation to investigate next; one [declared in code](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#declaring-objectives-in-code) names the handler that declares it (`declaredIn`). |
| `list_alert_rules`    | The [alert rules](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md) across every project you can see.                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `list_alert_events`   | The firing history, newest first. Filter by rule, project, state, severity, or a `since`/`until` window on when events started; page older history by passing the oldest `startedAt` you've seen as `until`.                                                         |
| `search`              | Full-text search over your projects, applications, alert rules, SLOs, and issues.                                                                                                                                                                                    |

### Diagnostics - regressions

| Tool               | What it answers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `find_regressions` | Releases (service versions) that made things worse: error rate and latency before vs. after each release boundary, classified better/worse/stable, with the specific operations each bad release degraded. Takes an optional `windowMinutes` for the comparison window either side of a boundary.                                                                        |
| `diff_release`     | What one release changed in the code: the queries, outbound calls and NestJS methods whose calls per request or own time per call moved across its boundary by more than noise - a new N+1, a call it started making, a method grown slow - ranked by the time each adds to an average request. Pass the `version` and `applicationId` you used with `find_regressions`. |

### Diagnostics - requests

| Tool                    | What it answers                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_slow_operations`  | The slowest HTTP operations in the window, p95-ranked, with volume alongside - so effort goes to what's slow _and_ hot.                                                                                                                   |
| `get_operation_details` | One route (`operationId`, optionally `method`): latency and error summary plus recent individual requests, each with duration, status, and `traceId`.                                                                                     |
| `get_trace`             | A `traceId` resolved to every execution that ran under it - across services, requests, and jobs - each with its span tree (name, duration, start offset, errors). The [waterfall](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#reading-the-waterfall). |
| `get_trace_logs`        | Every log line emitted under a `traceId`, in order: what the code said while that waterfall was happening.                                                                                                                                |

### Diagnostics - errors

| Tool                 | What it answers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_error_groups`  | Errors [grouped by fingerprint](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#grouping-errors-into-defects), ranked by occurrence count. Each group carries its class, a verbatim sample message and stack trace, first/last seen, and the release that introduced it. |
| `get_error_details`  | Recent occurrences of one error class: per-occurrence message, status, user, and `traceId`, plus a summary.                                                                                                                                                 |
| `get_error_trend`    | Whether errors are growing or decaying over the window, already classified as a direction. Scope it to one class to ask whether a specific bug is getting worse.                                                                                            |
| `get_affected_users` | The blast radius of one error class: which end users hit it and how often. Turns "an error exists" into "this many people are affected".                                                                                                                    |

### Diagnostics - jobs

| Tool              | What it answers                                                                                                                |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `list_jobs`       | Background job (queue worker) performance in the window, per job name and queue: volume, duration, and failure counts.         |
| `get_job_details` | One job name on one queue: duration and wait-time summaries plus recent individual executions, each with status and `traceId`. |

### Diagnostics - code and dependencies

| Tool                | What it answers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_classes`      | Where the time goes per NestJS class - controllers, providers, repositories - as on the [Services](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#services) page: own time, total time, calls, errors, and each class's share of all own time. Sorted by own time unless you ask for `totalDuration` or `callCount`. |
| `get_class_methods` | The methods of one class, with the same own/total split, calls, and errors: which method of a hot class is the hot one.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `get_service_map`   | Who calls whom across the project, as on the [Map](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#map): applications, queues, databases, and external hosts, with calls, errors, and the heaviest statements or endpoints behind each link. Always the whole project; `timeInterval` only.                           |

### Setting up a service

The path from "not instrumented" to "reporting". `list_applications` reads; the other three write, and each goes through the same service as the matching dashboard button, so your role on the project and your plan's limits apply exactly as they do there, and a refusal comes back as the tool's answer.

| Tool                 | What it does                                                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_applications`  | The applications of one project. Check it before creating a duplicate.                                                                                                    |
| `create_project`     | Creates a project, in an existing team (pass its id) or a new one named after the project.                                                                                |
| `create_application` | Registers one NestJS service in a project. The name sticks, and should match the `serviceId` you give the SDK.                                                            |
| `create_api_key`     | Issues the key pair the SDK authenticates with. The secret is returned once; a well-behaved client writes it to your git-ignored environment file and does not repeat it. |

With these an agent can take a repository from "not instrumented" to "reporting" in one request: _"Set up NestJS Observe for this service"_ becomes `list_projects` -> `create_application` -> `create_api_key`, then the install and the three code edits from the [SDK guide](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md).

### Resolving an issue

The one write outside setup, because the agent that just shipped the fix is the one thing that knows which release carries it. Left for someone to tick later, the version is guesswork and verification starts watching in the wrong place.

| Tool            | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `resolve_issue` | Marks an issue resolved after a fix ships, which starts [fix verification](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md#fix-verification) against the pre-incident baseline. Pass `fixedInVersion` to hold the watch until the release carrying the fix appears in telemetry. |

### What MCP cannot do

Nothing can be deleted, renamed or revoked over MCP. Issues can be resolved but not otherwise edited, and alert rules, SLOs and error-group status can't be changed at all - those stay in the dashboard. Whether more writes arrive is not yet decided.

Two smaller shapes worth knowing: tool results drop the time-bucketed chart series the dashboard endpoints return, because hundreds of bucket values cost context and say less than the summary derived from them. And `GET` and `DELETE` on `/mcp` answer 405 - both concern sessions, and this endpoint has none.

## When something fails

- **401** - the token is missing, expired, revoked, or the `Authorization` header is malformed. It must read `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, with a personal token (`omcp_...`) or a dashboard JWT. Check the token is still listed under [MCP tokens](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/dashboard/mcp-tokens).
- **405** - the client sent `GET` or `DELETE`. Every MCP request to this endpoint is a `POST`.
- **A tool result with `isError: true`** - the transport worked and the request was answered; the underlying read simply failed for an ordinary reason, such as "project not found" or no access to it. The message says which. A guessed project id coming back 404 is an answer for the agent, not a broken connection.

## Where to go next

- [Traces & spans](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md) - what `get_trace` returns, and the one-paste alternative for handing a single failure to a coding agent.
- [Telemetry](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md) - the dashboard views these tools read from.
- [Overview → Access control](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/overview.md#access-control) - the permissions a token inherits from you.

---

# Users

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/users

When your application reports a user identifier alongside its telemetry, **Users** turns the request stream into something you can reason about per person: who is using the project, who is hitting errors, and - on a single user's page - what they were actually trying to do when it happened.

This is not analytics for its own sake. It exists so that "a customer says checkout is broken" becomes a page you can open, rather than a search through raw request logs for anything with the right timestamp.

![Users overview](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/users/users.webp)

## Reporting a user

Users appear as soon as your applications attach a user identifier to their telemetry - see [SDK](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md). The identifier is whatever your system uses to mean "one person": a user id, an account id, a tenant-scoped id. The dashboard treats it as an opaque string and never tries to resolve it into a name, an email, or anything else you didn't send.

Requests without a user identifier are not lost - they simply don't appear in these views. Unauthenticated traffic behaves exactly as it should: it shows up under [Requests](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#requests) and nowhere here.

## The users overview

The **Users** view shows active users over the selected window as a chart, and a searchable table of everyone seen in it:

| Column           | What it tells you                        |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| User             | The identifier your application reported |
| Duration         | Average duration of this user's calls    |
| Failure rate     | Share of their calls that failed         |
| Count            | How many operations they performed       |
| Last interaction | When they were last seen                 |

Sorting by failure rate is the fastest way to find out whether an error spike is spread across everyone (a broken deploy) or concentrated in a handful of accounts (bad data, an unusual tenant, a permissions edge case). That distinction usually decides what you do next, and it's very hard to see from a route-level chart.

## Customers: users grouped into accounts

Sorting individual identities answers an engineer's question. It doesn't answer the one an account manager gets asked: _how is Acme doing?_ The **Group by customer** switch in the page header answers that instead, by grouping the identities you already report into the accounts they belong to.

![Customers](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/users/customers.webp)

The grouping rests on one observation: in a B2B product, user identities are work email addresses, so the domain behind them (`acme.com`) is the account. Nothing new has to be instrumented - it's the same telemetry, read one level up.

| Column     | What it tells you                                           |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Customer   | The domain the account is identified by                     |
| Users      | How many people from that account were seen in the window   |
| Requests   | Requests attributed to them                                 |
| Error rate | Share of those requests that failed                         |
| Worst p95  | The **worst** p95 among the account's users, not an average |
| Last seen  | When anyone from the account last interacted                |

Worst p95 is labelled that way everywhere it appears because it is genuinely a maximum, not a blend: an account manager should be able to quote the worst experience someone at that company had, and percentile sketches can't be re-rolled into an average once they've been reduced per user.

Two kinds of rows are folded away rather than listed as accounts: consumer email providers, and domains seen for only one person. Both would otherwise fill the table with a long tail that isn't a customer. The folded rows are still counted - the header's user and request totals include everything, so they reconcile with the [users overview](#the-users-overview), while the account count covers real accounts only.

Like the errors page's defect grouping, this is a switch rather than a second page - the same rows, the same chart, the same search box, read as companies instead of people - and the choice travels in the URL, so "here's how acme.com looks" is a link you can send.

## A single user

Opening a user shows everything they did in the selected window: operations, errors, failure rate, average duration, p95, and when they were last seen - the same summary shape as an operation page, scoped to a person instead of a route.

Beneath it are two things: the **Actions** card, which reconstructs what the user was doing, and the **Operations** table, which lists their individual requests. Every row in that table links straight to the [request detail page](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#requests), so the path from "this customer complained" to "here is the failing trace with the source code" is three clicks.

![User detail](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/users/single-user.webp)

## Actions: grouped requests

A flat list of requests answers "which endpoints were hit". It never answers "what did this person actually do", because a single click in a UI fans out into several API calls - a page load might fire five in 200ms.

The **Actions** card fixes that by grouping a user's calls by proximity in time: calls closer together than a gap threshold count as one action. Each group records when it started and ended, how long the whole burst took, how many of its calls failed, and how much idle time preceded it.

The **group within** control sets that threshold - 5s, 30s (the default), 2m, or 10m. It is a reading choice, not a filter: grouping happens in the browser on data already loaded, so changing it re-draws instantly rather than re-querying.

> [!INFO] 30 seconds is deliberately far tighter than the 30-minute window web analytics uses for a _visit_. The unit here is one action, not one sitting: long enough to hold a page load together with the lazy-loaded calls that follow it, short enough that reading a page and then clicking again reads as two actions rather than one long one.

Turn the gap up when you want the shape of a whole session; turn it down to 5s when you're trying to separate two clicks that happened in quick succession.

### Timeline

The default view draws each action as a horizontal track, most recent first, with every call positioned on the action's own clock and failures marked. Above each track is a summary of what the burst contained - the endpoints it hit, busiest first - so you can read a user's history without expanding anything.

A few deliberate choices in how it's drawn:

- **Marks are positioned truthfully; only their width is floored.** Most calls are milliseconds inside a burst that lasts seconds, so a strictly proportional mark would be sub-pixel. Dropping those calls would under-report what the user did, so they are drawn at a minimum width instead.
- **Very busy actions become a density strip.** A poll storm can put hundreds of calls into one burst, and hundreds of tiny links in a 22px track are neither clickable nor cheap to render. Past that density the track shades by activity instead - the same story, still readable.
- **Long histories render the most recent actions first**, with the rest behind a "show all". A heavy user's window can hold hundreds of actions, and the recent ones are the ones being investigated.

Clicking a track opens its **replay**: the action's calls revealed one at a time, in order, each with its real offset from the start of the burst, its duration, its status, and a link to its request. The animation carries the _order_; the printed offsets carry the _clock_ - real spacing inside a burst is milliseconds, so replaying in true time would just flash everything at once. Past a few dozen steps a step-by-step story stops being one, so the remainder is summarised in a footer.

This is the view for reconstructing a bug report. "It broke when I clicked save" becomes a specific burst, with the exact sequence of calls it produced, and the failing one highlighted in it.

![Actions timeline](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/users/timeline.webp)

### Paths

The **Paths** view aggregates the same actions into a flow chart: every consecutive pair of calls within an action becomes a directed step, summed across all of the user's actions in the window. The left column is what came first, the right column what followed, and the ribbon between them is thicker the more often that step happened.

- **Ribbons that mostly fail are drawn in red** - more than half of those steps ended in a 4xx or 5xx.
- **Only the busiest paths are drawn** (up to twelve), with the rest counted in a footer. Past a dozen ribbons the chart is a woven mat rather than a diagram, and the busy paths are the story.
- **Steps never cross an action boundary.** A gap between actions is, by definition, idle time; linking the last call of one action to the first call of the next would claim a causal step where the user demonstrably walked away. Because of that, the paths depend on the same **group within** setting as the timeline - both views share one grouping, so they can never disagree about what an action was.
- **Self-transitions are kept.** A burst of repeated calls to one endpoint - a poll, a retry loop - is real behaviour worth seeing, not noise to filter out.

![User paths](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/users/flow.webp)

### What the two views are for

| Question                                                    | View                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What did this customer do right before the error?           | Timeline, then replay the action                                  |
| Which exact call failed in that action?                     | Replay - each step links to its request                           |
| Is this user retrying the same endpoint over and over?      | Paths - a thick self-transition                                   |
| Does the failure always follow the same preceding call?     | Paths - a red ribbon out of one node                              |
| Is the client hammering an endpoint after a failure?        | Either - a dense burst in the timeline, a heavy loop in Paths     |
| Is this user's experience unusual, or is everyone affected? | The [users overview](#the-users-overview), sorted by failure rate |

The pattern to look for in Paths is a step that is both frequent and red: an endpoint that reliably fails _when reached from a particular predecessor_ is a much sharper lead than an endpoint with a 4% overall error rate, because it names the state the user was in.

## From a user to a fix

The views chain into the rest of the dashboard, and that's the point:

1. Find the user - from a support ticket, or from the failure-rate sort on the overview.
2. Open their **Actions** timeline and locate the burst that matches when the problem happened.
3. Replay it to find the exact call that failed.
4. Follow that call into its [request detail page](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#requests) - status, duration against the route's baseline, [error with source code](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#errors-with-source-code), waterfall, and logs.
5. [Copy the agent prompt](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#hand-it-to-a-coding-agent) and hand it to a coding agent, or open an [issue](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md) linked to the request so the context travels with the work.

## Availability

The Actions card only renders when the user activity feed is available for your project; where it isn't, the rest of the user page - summary and operations table - works normally. Nothing else on the page depends on it.

Reporting user identifiers is optional and entirely under your control: send only what you're comfortable storing, and prefer an opaque internal id over anything personally identifying.

---

# Profiler

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/profiler

Requests, jobs, and traces tell you how your application behaved. The **Profiler** tells you how the process underneath was doing while it behaved that way - CPU, memory, event loop, and garbage collection, sampled from inside your running Node processes.

The two answer different questions, and you usually need both. A route that got slower with no change to its span timings is not a slow route; it's a process that couldn't get scheduled. That is invisible in a trace and obvious here.

![Profiler](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/profiler.webp)

## Scope: application and instance

Runtime metrics are reported **per application**, and it makes no sense to average an API server's heap against a worker's. So the Profiler always resolves to one application: pick one in the [params bar](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#filtering-the-params-bar), or the page picks one for you and says which - a page that looked project-wide while showing one service's numbers would be worse than one that admits its scope.

When an application runs on more than one instance (multiple pods, multiple processes), a **service node** selector appears alongside an **Instances** card comparing the nodes against each other on CPU, memory, and event loop lag. Selecting a node narrows every chart on the page to that process.

That comparison matters more than it looks. Averaged across ten pods, one pod pinned at 100% CPU is a 10% blip; per instance it is an outage in progress. Uneven load is also the signature of a specific class of bug - a sticky load balancer, a consumer that grabbed every partition, a leader-election loop that never rotated.

## What the charts show

| Chart                      | Reads as                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Memory**                 | RSS, heap total, and heap used over time. The three nest (`heapUsed ≤ heapTotal ≤ rss`), so the gaps between them are readable: heap growing inside a flat RSS is ordinary; RSS growing away from the heap points at buffers or native memory |
| **Memory utilization %**   | Heap used against the process's ceiling - the number that predicts an OOM kill                                                                                                                                                                |
| **CPU**                    | CPU time consumed by the process                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **CPU utilization %**      | That time against what was available, which is the one to alert on                                                                                                                                                                            |
