| **Event loop delay**       | How long the loop is running behind schedule. Direct latency: every pending callback, including your HTTP responses, waits this long before it even starts                                                                                    |
| **Event loop utilization** | The share of time the loop had work in hand. Near 1.0 means saturated - more traffic will not go faster, it will only queue                                                                                                                   |
| **GC duration**            | Time spent in garbage collection. Wall-clock time your code was not running                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **GC count**               | Collection frequency, split by kind - frequent minor collections are normal, frequent major ones are not                                                                                                                                      |

The event loop pair is the most diagnostic thing on the page for a Node service. Delay and utilization rising _together_ is the shape of synchronous work blocking the loop - a heavy JSON parse, a crypto call, a tight loop on the hot path. High utilization with flat delay is just a busy, healthy process.

## Clicking into a spike

The Memory and Event loop delay charts are clickable. Click any point - a spike or otherwise - and a drawer opens asking **What ran here?**: the requests and jobs that ran in that moment, ranked by how far each one's rate or duration strayed from its own baseline over the page's window, not by raw volume. A ratio badge on each row reads as "×12 rate" or "×3.1 slower" ("first seen here" for an operation that didn't run in the baseline at all), and every row links straight to that operation's Requests or Jobs detail page.

Only genuine outliers make the list - an operation needs at least 3 calls in that moment and at least 1.5x its baseline to show up. If nothing was unusual, the drawer says so: whatever moved the chart came from garbage collection, a sibling process, or the host itself, not from anything in your operation list.

CPU, GC, and the utilization-percentage charts don't have this yet - the ranking needs a rate/duration baseline to compare against, which only Memory and Event loop delay carry cleanly enough right now.

![Spike](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/telemetry/spike.webp)

## Suggestions

The Profiler evaluates a few rules against the data already on the page and surfaces a notice when one matches, rather than expecting you to spot the shape yourself:

| Notice                                                 | Fires when                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Resource utilization is high / Running out of headroom | CPU or memory above 85% (elevated) or 95% (critical)                                                                                                       |
| Heap usage keeps climbing                              | Mean heap in the last third of the window is 30%+ above the first third - compared in thirds so a normal allocate/collect sawtooth can't look like a trend |
| The event loop is falling behind                       | Delay and utilization both rising versus the previous period, past a floor of 50ms and 0.7                                                                 |
| Garbage collection is taking real time                 | GC accounts for more than 5% of the window                                                                                                                 |
| One instance is doing most of the work                 | One node past 70%, with a 30-point spread to the others                                                                                                    |

The heap-growth rule earns its place next to the 85% threshold: saturation fires when memory is _already_ nearly gone, minutes from an OOM kill. A heap walking steadily upward is the same story caught while there's still time to fix it.

Dismissing a notice keeps it dismissed for the rest of your session, so a rule you've already read doesn't follow you around while you work. A new session, or a change in severity, is new information and shows again.

## Turning a reading into an alert

Everything here can be watched continuously instead of by eye. The Runtime family of [alert rules](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md#what-a-rule-watches) covers event loop delay, CPU usage, and memory usage, scoped to an application and sampled per process. Anomaly detection is often the better mode for these: a fixed CPU threshold that's right for one service is wrong for the next, but "unlike its own recent baseline" travels.

## Working with the rest of the dashboard

The Profiler answers _whether_ the process was struggling. To find out _what it was doing_, cross-reference:

1. Note the window where the metric moved.
2. Open [Requests](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#requests) or [Jobs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#jobs) for the same window and application. Did throughput spike, or did latency rise with throughput flat? The first is load; the second is the process losing ground. On the Memory or Event loop delay chart, [clicking the point itself](#clicking-into-a-spike) does this lookup for you.
3. Check [Releases](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#releases). A step change that lines up with a deploy is a regression, not a capacity problem.
4. Open a slow execution from that window and read its [waterfall](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#reading-the-waterfall). A trace whose spans are all _individually_ fast but whose total is long is the fingerprint of event loop delay - the time is between the spans, not in them.

Coming from the other direction - you have a slow operation and want to know whether the process was to blame - an operation's page runs this comparison for you and states the result: see [Was the process to blame?](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#was-the-process-to-blame).

## Billing and retention

Profiling data is not billed as [Observability Events](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md) - it's a plan capability, not a metered stream. It's also retained for a shorter window than the rest of your telemetry, on the reasoning that runtime metrics are for diagnosing a recent regression, not for archaeology.

---

# Alerts

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/alerts

Alerts get you told when your telemetry crosses a threshold you care about, instead of you finding out from a customer. Alert rules are available on Pro, Scale, and Enterprise.

![Alert rules](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/alerts/rules.webp)

## What a rule watches

A rule watches one **metric**, drawn from one of a few families:

| Family  | Metrics                                          | Scoped to                                           |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Request | Error rate, p95 latency, avg latency, throughput | An application, and optionally one route + method   |
| Job     | Job failure rate, job throughput, p95 queue wait | An application, and optionally one job name + queue |
| Absence | Telemetry silence, job silence                   | An application, or one job name + queue             |
| Logs    | Matching log lines                               | A pattern, and optionally levels + logger context   |
| Errors  | New error groups                                 | An application, or the whole project                |
| Runtime | Event loop delay, CPU usage, memory usage        | An application (sampled per process)                |
| Custom  | Any custom metric your application reports       | A metric name, and optionally one label             |
| SLO     | SLO burn rate                                    | The SLO itself - see below                          |

Leaving the operation unset watches the whole application rather than a single route or job.

## Absence detection

Every metric above fires on data that arrived and crossed a line. **Telemetry silence** and **Job silence** fire on data that stopped arriving at all - your app went quiet, or a cron didn't run.

- **Telemetry silence** watches an application's runtime heartbeat - the same profiler samples that flow even when the app is otherwise idle - and fires once it's been silent longer than the tolerance you set (2 minutes to 7 days). There's no threshold number to reason about here beyond that duration: the rule fires the moment silence exceeds it, and resolves the moment data resumes.
- **Job silence** does the same for one job, identified by name and optionally narrowed to a queue. Leave both blank to watch whether _any_ job in the project has run recently.

Both read "silent for over 15 min" rather than a metric crossing a threshold, because that's the honest description of what happened - nothing was read at all. A scope that has never reported _anything_ doesn't fire: "not yet integrated" isn't "down," and the rule simply waits for its first reading before it starts the clock. When a silence rule does fire, its firing history shows how long the gap ran and exactly when data was last seen.

This is both lightweight uptime monitoring (no external probe needed - your own runtime metrics are the heartbeat) and Sentry-Crons-style job monitoring, from the same mechanism. The same "last seen" signal also drives the badge on each application's card in [Applications](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/applications.md), so a silence you'd notice from an alert is visible ambiently too.

## New errors

A **new error groups** rule fires when an error Observe has never seen before appears - a new fingerprint, not a recurrence of a known one. "Above 0" over a short window is the canonical rule.

It counts **unhandled failures only**: a group whose first occurrence answered 5xx, or that failed on an entry point with no HTTP status at all (an RPC handler, a gateway message). A failed job doesn't open an error group - watch jobs with a [job failure rate](#what-a-rule-watches) rule. An error your code threw on purpose - a `NotFoundException`, a failed validation, a wrong password - still appears in the [Errors](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#errors) list, but it is not a new bug, and a rule that fires the first time a crawler requests a page that doesn't exist teaches its owner to ignore it. Groups you marked _ignored_, and groups your error filters mark _expected_, are never counted.

### The built-in new-error email

Every plan, Free included, gets this without creating a rule: when a project reports an unhandled error it has never seen before, its members get one email listing the new errors (up to five, then "+N more"), at most six emails per project per day. Turn it off for yourself under **Settings → New error emails**; every email's footer links there. A project that already has its own _new error groups_ rule with an email channel is skipped, so nobody is told twice.

## Log-pattern alerts

**Matching log lines** counts how many log lines contain a substring within the evaluation window, and fires when that count crosses a threshold - "alert me when `payment declined` appears more than 10 times in 15 minutes." The pattern is a plain substring match, case-insensitive, never a regular expression; it needs at least 3 characters, since anything shorter can't use the search index that makes the check cheap. Optionally narrow by log level or logger context (Nest's `[PaymentsService]` label).

The rule builder shows a live preview - "would have matched 37 lines in the last hour" - against the same filters the rule will evaluate, so you're not guessing whether a pattern is too broad or too narrow before saving it. When the rule fires, the event carries up to five of the matching lines (message, context, timestamp, trace) so you can see what tripped it without leaving the alert.

Log-pattern alerts require a plan with logs streaming - see [Billing & usage](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md).

## Queue wait alerts

Job failure-rate alerts tell you after a backlog has already burned through; **p95 queue wait** tells you while it's growing. It watches how long jobs sit enqueued before a worker picks them up, at the 95th percentile, and can be scoped to one job, one queue, or both. It behaves like any other windowed metric - normal comparisons, normal evaluation windows - and points at the same queue-wait chart shown on a job's detail page in [Telemetry](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#jobs).

## Threshold vs. anomaly detection

Every rule runs in one of two modes:

- **Fixed threshold** - fires when the metric goes **above** or **below** a number you set (e.g. "error rate above 5%").
- **Anomaly detection** - fires when the metric deviates from its own recent baseline by more than a **sensitivity**, expressed in sigma-equivalents (default 3.5, valid from 1 upward). Here "above" means a spike over the baseline and "below" means a collapse under it - there's no fixed number to reason about, just how unusual the behavior is relative to normal for that metric.

Silence, log-pattern, and queue-wait rules are threshold-only - a duration or a count has no baseline to deviate from, so anomaly mode isn't offered for them.

## Evaluation window

A rule evaluates over a rolling window - 5, 10, 15, 30, 60, or 180 minutes. Shorter than 5 minutes isn't offered: below that, a single slow call can move a p95 reading enough to fire on nothing. (SLO burn-rate rules get longer windows too - see [SLOs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/slos.md#burn-rate-alerts).) Silence rules don't use a window at all - each check is "how old is the newest data," not "what happened over the last N minutes" - so the builder replaces it with the tolerance described [above](#absence-detection).

## Severity and channels

Every rule has a **severity** - Low, Medium, High, or Critical - carried onto anything the rule triggers downstream, including an issue if you route it to one. A rule can notify through any combination of:

- **Email**
- **Slack**, via an incoming webhook URL from your Slack workspace
- **Webhook**, a generic HTTP callback to any endpoint you control
- **Create issue**, opening an [issue](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md) automatically, pre-filled with the rule's severity and scope
- **In-app**, showing up in your notifications feed

![Create alert](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/alerts/create-alert.webp)

## Quiet hours

Any rule can carry a recurring mute schedule - a staging project that goes quiet overnight, a batch window that's expected to be noisy, a maintenance slot you don't want paging anyone. Turn on **Mute on a schedule** and add one or more windows: the days it starts on, a from/to time, and the timezone the times are read in.

A window's days are the days it _starts_ on, not every day it covers. An overnight window - 22:00 to 06:00 - ticked for Monday runs quiet until Tuesday morning; ticking Tuesday as well would additionally silence Tuesday evening, which is a different schedule. The builder reads each window back as a sentence ("Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri 22:00 → 06:00 next day") so this is never left to be inferred from two time fields. **Weeknights** and **Weekends** presets cover the common cases in one click.

Times are wall-clock in the timezone you pick, not a fixed offset - daylight saving is handled from the zone name, so a schedule set once doesn't drift or need re-editing twice a year. The picker defaults to your browser's own timezone.

**Muted is its own state, not "OK."** While a window is open, the rule keeps evaluating but notifies nobody; a rule that was already firing when the window opened stays firing rather than being marked healthy, and resumes notifying the moment the window closes. The rule's status chip reads **Muted** (or **Firing · muted** if it's mid-incident) so a quiet rule is never mistaken for a healthy one.

## While overage is paused

When [spike protection or a monthly overage budget](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#while-overage-is-paused) pauses the overage of the account that pays for a project, the project keeps only its server errors past the account's included events - and a $0 budget's stop keeps nothing. Read against that, an error rate looks like 100%, throughput collapses and jobs seem to stop, so the rules that read requests, jobs or logs are skipped until the pause lifts: error rate, p95 and avg latency, throughput, job failure rate, job throughput, p95 queue wait, telemetry silence, job silence, matching log lines and SLO burn rate.

Skipped is stricter than muted: nothing is compared at all, and each rule keeps the state it had when the pause began. **New error groups**, runtime metric and custom metric rules keep running, though during a $0 budget's stop nothing new arrives for them to read.

## History

A firing rule moves through states - **OK → Firing → Resolved** - and every transition is recorded, quiet hours included: a rule's detail page shows its mute schedule alongside its condition, so "why didn't this page anyone" is answered on the same screen as "what does this watch." **Alert history** shows every firing across every project, with the delivery status (delivered, pending, failed) of each channel it notified.

![Alert history](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/alerts/history.webp)

## SLO burn-rate alerts

A burn-rate alert is a regular alert rule pointed at an [SLO](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/slos.md) instead of a raw metric - its threshold is a multiple of the SLO's sustainable burn rate rather than a reading, so "above 14.4×" means "burning the error budget fast enough to exhaust a 28-day objective in about two days." Create one from an SLO's detail page; scope, comparison, and detection mode are fixed by the SLO itself, so the form only asks for the multiple and the window.

---

# SLOs

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/slos

SLOs turn "error rate above 5%" into "we promised 99.9% and we're spending the budget too fast." They're objectives over telemetry you're already collecting - no new instrumentation required. SLOs are available on Scale and Enterprise, with up to 50 per project.

![SLO list](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/slos/slos.webp)

## The model

An SLO is built from three layered ideas:

- **SLI (service level indicator)** - a ratio of good events to total events, over a window. Not a raw reading: "fraction of requests under 300ms" is an SLI, "p95 latency" is not.
- **Objective** - the SLI plus a target percentage (90–99.999%) over a rolling compliance window (7, 14, 28, or 30 days).
- **Error budget** - how much room you have to miss the target, derived as `1 − target`. **Burn rate** is how fast that budget is being spent: a burn rate of 1.0 means spending it exactly on schedule to run out right at the end of the window; 14.4 means the whole 28-day budget would be gone in about two days at the current rate.

## SLI kinds

| Kind         | A "good" event is...                               |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Availability | A request that didn't produce an unhandled error   |
| Latency      | A request that completed under a threshold you set |
| Job success  | A job run that completed rather than failed        |

By default, a handled error still counts as good - it produced a response the caller could use. You can flip that per SLO if a handled-error-as-4xx genuinely means broken for your service.

An SLO can watch a whole project, one application, or narrow further to a single route or job, exactly like an alert rule's scope.

## Declared in code

An SLO can also be declared next to the route it covers, with the SDK's `@Objective()` decorator - see [Declaring objectives in code](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#declaring-objectives-in-code). Each promise the decorator makes becomes an SLO like any other, except that the code owns it: the list marks it **in code**, its page names the handler and the release that last declared it, and its objective changes when the decorator does - on the next deploy - rather than in the dashboard.

## No traffic isn't failure

If a window has no events at all, the SLI reads as "no traffic" rather than 100% (which would hide a dead service behind a green SLO) or 0% (which would page you every quiet night). No budget is burned during a window with nothing to measure.

## Reading the detail page

An SLO's detail page shows its objective as a plain sentence ("99.9% of requests under 300ms, rolling 28 days"), its current SLI, a budget bar (rendered as explicitly over-budget when it's gone negative, never clamped to empty), and burn rate over the last 1, 6, and 24 hours. Below that: a chart of the SLI against its target line, a budget staircase over time, and any burn-rate alert rules watching this SLO along with their recent firings.

![SLO detail](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/slos/slo-detail.webp)

## Burn-rate alerts

Create an alert straight from an SLO's detail page - see [Alerts → SLO burn-rate alerts](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md#slo-burn-rate-alerts) for how the threshold and window work. A few starting points:

| Policy    | Window  | Threshold | Catches                                 |
| --------- | ------- | --------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Fast burn | 1 hour  | 14.4×     | 2% of a 28-day budget gone in one hour  |
| Slow burn | 6 hours | 6×        | 5% of a 28-day budget gone in six hours |
| Trickle   | 3 days  | 1×        | Steadily on track to miss the objective |

Deleting an SLO deletes any burn-rate alert rules built on it - they have nothing left to watch.

While the account that pays for the project has its overage [paused or stopped](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#while-overage-is-paused), those minutes are left out of the SLO: they don't count toward its compliance or spend its error budget, and they show as a gap on its chart. A pause keeps only server errors, so counting them would read as an outage the service never had. Burn-rate rules are skipped meanwhile, like every rule that reads requests or jobs - see [Alerts → While overage is paused](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md#while-overage-is-paused).

## Retention is the ceiling

A compliance window can't exceed how long your plan retains telemetry: on Scale (90 days), every window option is available; a 90-day plan can measure a 28-day objective, but a plan retaining less than 28 days can't offer that window.

---

# Issues

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/issues

Issues are lightweight, project-scoped tracking for the work that comes out of your telemetry - a recurring error worth fixing, a latency regression to investigate, a follow-up from an incident. Create them by hand, or automatically from an [alert rule](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md#severity-and-channels) using the "Create issue" channel.

![Issues list](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/issues/issues.webp)

## Creating an issue

An issue has a title, description, severity (Low, Medium, High, Critical - the same scale alerts use), an assignee, and an optional due date. You can attach files and link the issue to the request, error, job, or trace it came from, so anyone opening it later has the telemetry in context, not just a description of it.

## Status

An issue moves through a fixed set of statuses as work on it progresses:

| Status      | Meaning                            |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Open        | Not yet started                    |
| In progress | Actively being worked              |
| Blocked     | Stopped, waiting on something else |
| On hold     | Deliberately paused                |
| Review      | Work is done, awaiting review      |
| Resolved    | Fixed                              |
| Verifying   | Fixed, and we're watching to confirm it held |
| Closed      | Done, no further action            |

Blocked and on hold are both mid-flight but distinct: blocked is involuntary (waiting on a dependency), on hold is a choice. Neither counts as closed, so the open-issues count and the default list view include both. Verifying is also active work, not a form of done - it sits with the in-flight statuses everywhere, including the open-issues count.

## Incident record

Every issue linked to telemetry opens with its **incident record**: the account of what happened, assembled from what the issue links to rather than typed up afterwards.

- **What** - the error class, route or job the issue is about, and the alert rule that raised it if one did, linked to its page.
- **When** - from the first sign of it to its end: the alert firing, or the error class's first sighting if that was within the week before the issue was filed, or else the execution the issue was filed from. It ends when the fix is confirmed, or when the issue is closed or resolved with nothing left to watch; until then it reads as ongoing.
- **Introduced in** - the release that first reported the error class. For an issue with no error class, the record names the newest release deployed in the day before it began instead - as a suspect, with that release's own verdict alongside, never as a cause.
- **Affected** - how many users hit it, and the customer companies behind them, grouped by their email domains the way [Customers](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/users.md#customers-users-grouped-into-accounts) groups them. For an issue about a route rather than an error class, it counts the users whose requests to that route failed, over the incident's first day.
- **Fix** - the release the fix shipped in, when it deployed, and whether [verification](#fix-verification) confirmed it.

Under the facts is a timeline of those moments, from the release to the confirmation. **Copy summary** puts the whole record on your clipboard as plain text, for the postmortem, the status update or the note to a customer that follows an incident.

## Fix verification

When you mark an issue resolved, you can optionally say **which release fixes it went out in**. If the issue names something measurable - an operation, an alert rule's scope - we don't just take your word for it: we watch that operation's telemetry against how it behaved before the incident, and tell you whether the fix actually held.

![Fix verification](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/issues/verification.webp)

**Marking as resolved.** The "Fixed in version" field is optional. Naming a release holds verification until that release actually shows up in telemetry - useful when you're resolving the issue before deploying the fix. Leaving it blank starts watching immediately, against whatever's live right now.

If there's something to watch, the issue moves to **Verifying** instead of Resolved - reflecting what actually happened, not what you asked for. From there it resolves itself one of three ways:

- **Confirmed** - readings have stayed inside the pre-incident baseline for long enough. The issue closes on its own.
- **Reopened** - a reading moved outside baseline again. The issue goes back to **Open**, with the reading that broke it recorded in the timeline.
- **Unverified** - after 7 days, nothing conclusive turned up (usually too little traffic on the operation to judge either way). This is neither a pass nor a failure - just an honest "we couldn't tell." Close the issue by hand if you're satisfied the fix is good.

A confirmation needs both a run of consecutive clean readings *and* two full evaluation windows of elapsed time to have passed - so on a busy endpoint this typically takes a few hours, and longer on a quiet one. Readings are taken every 5 minutes. A single inconclusive reading (too little traffic in that window) isn't treated as bad news or as progress - it's a pause, not a signal either way.

**Not every issue can be verified.** If the issue doesn't name an operation or alert rule, or the metric it's tied to has no baseline to compare against (a heartbeat, a log match), or there isn't enough pre-incident history to judge against, resolving it leaves a quiet note instead of starting a watch - the issue stays Resolved, and you close it by hand when you're ready.

## Activity and comments

Every issue has an activity feed recording status changes, assignment changes, and comments from anyone with access to the project - a running history of how the issue was worked, not just its current state.

![Issue detail](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/issues/issue-detail.webp)

## Linking from an alert

When an alert rule's channel is set to "Create issue," a firing rule opens an issue automatically, pre-filled with the rule's severity and a link back to the metric and scope it was watching - so the person who picks it up starts from the same context the alert had.

---

# Billing & usage

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/billing

Usage is metered in **Observability Events (OEs)** - one per request, background job run, error, log entry, or trace span your applications report. These compound rather than collapse into each other: a request that ran three service spans, wrote two log lines, and raised one error is seven events, not one. Every record counts the same regardless of kind - a span costs exactly as much as a request. The SDK's database query and outbound HTTP spans are the exception: they describe a span you already sent, so they [aren't billed](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#database-queries-and-outbound-http). Your plan sets a monthly allowance of included events, a retention window for how long that telemetry is kept, and what features are unlocked.

## Plans

| Plan       | Monthly | Included events | Retention  | Logs | Alerts | SSO | Seats      |
| ---------- | ------: | --------------: | ---------- | ---- | ------ | --- | ---------- |
| Free       |      $0 |            300k | 3 days     | ✗    | ✗      | ✗   | 1          |
| Pro        |     $29 |             25M | 30 days    | ✓    | ✓      | ✗   | 5          |
| Scale      |     $99 |            200M | 90 days    | ✓    | ✓      | ✓   | Unlimited  |
| Enterprise |  Custom |      Negotiated | Negotiated | ✓    | ✓      | ✓   | Negotiated |

Every plan, including Free, includes error monitoring, distributed tracing, and auto-instrumentation. Logs streaming, alerting, and team management start on Pro; SSO, [SLOs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/slos.md), and continuous [profiling](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#profiler) start on Scale. Annual billing is discounted 25% against the monthly price.

![Plans](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/billing/plans.webp)

Pro and Scale allow overage instead of a hard stop - $0.60 and $0.40 per additional million events, respectively - so a busy month doesn't mean lost telemetry. To keep overage from turning into a bill you didn't plan for, [spike protection](#spike-protection) pauses it when your usage surges, and a [monthly overage budget](#monthly-overage-budget) pauses it at an amount you choose. Free has no overage, so its allowance is a limit, and it applies in stages rather than all at once.

### Free plan limits

Requests, jobs and errors keep being recorded right up to the last of these stages. What goes first is the waterfall behind each trace:

- **A paced day.** Once your apps send 30,000 events in one UTC day - a tenth of the month's allowance - most waterfalls are paused until 00:00 UTC, so one noisy day can't spend the month. The spans held back don't count toward your allowance. The dashboard shows **Waterfalls paused** while it lasts, and the Usage page says how many events pausing has saved.
- **Reduced ingest, past 300k events.** Once the allowance is spent, charts stay live but most traces arrive without their spans, and each project's [rate cap](#spend-controls) comes down to 1,000 events a minute.
- **Refused, at 600k events.** At twice the allowance - counted on everything your apps send, including the spans reduced ingest dropped - the collector refuses new telemetry with a `429` until the next period. It's dropped, not queued.

On a paced day and in reduced ingest, server errors, failed jobs and anything over 1 s keep their full traces. A paced day ends at 00:00 UTC and the other two stages at the next period; upgrading ends all three.

### Spike protection

Spike protection pauses overage when your usage surges, before the rest of the month is billed at that pace. It's on by default on Pro. On Scale it's on for your first month on the plan - from checkout to the same day the next month - and off after that unless you keep it on. Free has no overage to protect, and Enterprise overage is agreed in your contract, so neither has it. Switch it on or off - or keep Scale's on past the first month - under **Overage controls** on **Billing → Spend controls**.

It only acts once your account is past its included events, and only when this month's overage, at today's pace, would come to $50 or more. On top of that:

- **In your first month on the plan**, nothing else is needed - spike or not. A steady pace that runs through the included events in the first weeks never looks like a spike against its own average, and it's exactly the bill this exists to stop.
- **After the first month**, today has to have already stored five normal days' worth of events. A normal day is your average over the last seven days, and never less than your plan's daily share of its included events. It counts what today has actually stored, not a projection, so a burst in a day's first minutes can't set it off - and the bigger the surge, the sooner it fires.

Once you resume collection, spike protection doesn't pause again until the 1st. While a [monthly overage budget](#monthly-overage-budget) is set, spike protection steps aside: the budget decides when overage pauses.

### Monthly overage budget

A monthly overage budget caps what overage can cost in a month. Set one on Pro or Scale under **Overage controls** on **Billing → Spend controls**, as a whole amount in your account's currency; there's none until you set one.

- **Above $0**, overage pauses once the month's overage reaches the budget. A budget at or below this month's overage so far pauses it at once.
- **At $0**, nothing past your included events is collected. Once they're used, collection stops - server errors included - until 00:00 UTC on the 1st, or until you raise or remove the budget. Overage already used this month is still billed. Agents are answered with a `429` and `Retry-After: 300`: they back off and try again every 5 minutes, so collection resumes within five minutes of the budget changing.

### While overage is paused

A paused account keeps what you need to see an incident, and drops the rest:

- **Kept, and not billed.** Server errors - requests that answered 5xx, failed jobs, and other executions that ended in an error - without their span trees. Runtime metrics, custom metrics and objectives keep flowing too.
- **Dropped, and not billed.** Everything else past your included events - other requests and jobs, every trace, and every log line, error-level ones included - is dropped, not queued. 4xx responses aren't kept: floods of `401`s and `429`s are a common cause of surges.
- **When it lifts.** At 00:00 UTC on the 1st, when the included events reset - or sooner, when you resume full collection for the rest of the month, set, raise or remove a monthly overage budget, switch spike protection off (for its own pauses), or upgrade to a plan whose included events cover the month so far. A budget at or below this month's overage pauses again at once, and a $0 budget's stop can't be resumed: only changing the budget or upgrading ends it before the 1st.
- **Who can act.** The account's billing owner, from the Usage or Spend controls page or the banner on any of its projects' pages, and the admins of its projects, from the banner on those projects' pages. When an admin acts, the owner gets an email saying so. Other members of its projects see a notice that collection is paused and until when, without figures or buttons.
- **Who's told.** The billing owner and the admins of the account's projects get an email when a pause or a stop starts.
- **On the Usage page,** a banner says why overage is paused and what the pause has kept off your bill, and the month's forecast holds where the month stands: what a pause drops isn't billed.
- **Alerts.** Rules that read requests, jobs or logs are skipped while the account is paused or stopped, SLO burn-rate rules included - a pause keeps only server errors, so they'd read it as an outage. See [Alerts](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md#while-overage-is-paused).
- **SLOs.** The minutes the account was paused or stopped are left out of its projects' SLOs - neither compliance nor the error budget counts them - and show as a gap on the SLO's chart. See [SLOs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/slos.md).
- **Agents.** Agents that support errors-only mode send only what a pause keeps, and say so in their logs; older agents keep sending everything, and the collector keeps only the server errors. See [SDK](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#when-overage-is-paused).

## Usage

The **Usage** page tracks your account's Observability Events for the current billing period against your plan's allowance, broken down by project, with a monthly trend so you can see whether a project's volume is growing before it becomes a surprise on the invoice.

![Usage](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/billing/usage.webp)

**What counts as an event.** Every retained record is one Observability Event: a request, a job, an error, a log line, and every span your application's own code produced. The one exception is the agent's **database-query and outbound-HTTP spans** (`pg`, `mysql2`, `mssql`, `mongodb`, `http`): they are detail about a method span you already sent, and they multiply - ten queries in one request would otherwise be ten more events - so they are recorded, shown in the waterfall, and **not counted** toward your allowance, your overage or your rate cap.

Set **quota notifications** - up to five thresholds, as a percentage of your allowance (e.g. 50%, 80%, 100%, or above 100% on an overage plan) - to get an email the moment your usage crosses one, rather than finding out at the invoice. Each threshold fires once per billing period and re-arms at the next.

On Pro and Scale, [spike protection](#spike-protection) and the [monthly overage budget](#monthly-overage-budget) are set on **Billing → Spend controls**.

## Cost attribution

Spend controls tell you what removed events; **Cost attribution** tells you which routes and jobs are behind the events still arriving, so you know what to remove. It's its own page - **Billing → Cost attribution**, right under Usage - scoped to one project at a time via the picker in the header, and always the current billing month, since that's the only period a spend decision can act on.

![Cost attribution](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/billing/cost-attribution.webp)

The top of the page states three numbers plainly rather than implying them:

- **Metered events** - from the same ingestion counters the invoice is built from.
- **Attributed** - the share the drivers below can actually explain. This is expected to land well under 100%: spans and logs carry no route or job name, so no driver can ever claim them, and the gap is called out rather than hidden.
- **Estimated overage**, or **Allowance** while you're still inside it.

Below that, a **Top drivers** table ranks routes and jobs by event volume, each with its share of the attributed total and what removing it would save. That saving is capped at the account's actual overage - a 10M-event route on an account that's 1M over the allowance shows the price of 1M, not 10M, because that's genuinely all it costs today. While the account is inside its allowance, every row shows a share of quota instead of a dollar figure: removing traffic there buys headroom, it doesn't lower an invoice that isn't happening.

**Drop filter** next to a row opens a confirmation with the exact pattern it will silence, then adds it to that project's [spend controls](#spend-controls) - the same drop-filter list, arrived at from the cost side instead of the controls side. Spans have no route to filter by, so the unattributed total offers **Span sampling** instead. Errors are never offered for filtering, on either page - they're low-volume, and they're the records you want when something breaks.

## Spend controls

Spend controls act at ingestion, before anything is metered - an event a control removes is never billed. They're configured per project on **Billing → Spend controls**, which lists each project's sampling, rate cap and drop filters beside the account's overage controls - or from the Usage page, next to that project's row in the by-project breakdown.

![Spend controls](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/docs/billing/spend-controls.webp)

- **Span sampling** - keep a fixed share of spans (50% or 25%) for a noisy project. Deeper rates (10% and 5%) are available on Enterprise plans - get in touch if you need them. Sampling is trace-coherent (a trace keeps all of its spans or none of them) and applies to spans only - requests, jobs, errors, and logs are never sampled, since silently dropping an individual error to save a fraction of a cent isn't a trade worth making automatically.
- **Rate caps** - a per-project ceiling on events per minute, for the deploy that goes wrong at 3am. It's a circuit breaker on rate; what a month's overage may cost is set by the account's [monthly overage budget](#monthly-overage-budget). The cap counts events after drop filters and span sampling have run, in the same unit as your bill - so sampling also lowers how close you run to it. Once a minute's cap is reached, the collector refuses the agent's batches with a `429` until the minute rolls over; the agent logs `Telemetry rate-limited (429)` and discards what it collects while paused. Unlike sampling and filters, a cap doesn't pick and choose: **everything in a refused batch is lost, errors included**. Set it well above your normal peak, and use sampling or filters to bring routine volume down.
- **Drop filters** - discard events at the edge that match a pattern, e.g. requests to `/health*`, so routine health-check traffic never becomes billable in the first place. Filters never match errors, for the same reason sampling never touches them.

Every control reports what it saved this billing period, so you can tell whether it's worth keeping. Changes apply going forward only - nothing already ingested is re-billed or removed retroactively.

---

# FAQ

Source: https://www.observe.nestjs.com/documentation/faq

## What is NestJS Observe?

An auto-instrumented observability platform built specifically for NestJS. Install the [SDK](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md), add a project API key, and your application starts streaming requests, jobs, errors, logs, and traces to a dashboard - no collector to run, no schema to design, no dashboards to build by hand. See [Overview](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/overview.md) for how accounts, teams, projects, and applications fit together.

## Can I see it before I install anything?

Yes - the [live demo](https://www.observe-demo.nestjs.com/dashboard) is the whole dashboard running over a generated dataset from a busy service: real request volumes, traces with waterfalls, errors, jobs and alerts. No signup, no credit card, nothing to install. It runs entirely in your browser, so nothing you do there touches an account.

## What makes it different?

Auto-instrumentation is built around Nest's own request lifecycle - controllers, interceptors, guards, queue consumers - rather than a generic Node.js agent bolted onto the framework. That's also why the [Services](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#services) view can show you time spent per NestJS class and method, in the vocabulary you wrote the code in, instead of only per HTTP route.

## How does the SDK work?

`ObserveModule.forRoot()` wires up automatic instrumentation for HTTP, RPC, gRPC, and job/queue consumers the moment your app boots - requests, errors, and traces show up in the dashboard within moments of your app receiving traffic, with no manual span wiring. `TracerService` is there for the rest: adding your own spans, capturing errors you handled yourself, and reporting custom metrics. See [SDK](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md) for the full setup.

## Can I use it with an existing app?

Yes. Run `npx @nestjs/observe link` in the app's directory: it installs the [SDK](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md), wires it into your root module and `main.ts`, and fetches an [API key](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/applications.md#api-keys) into `.env` - and NestJS Observe starts collecting traces, logs, and errors from your existing application without any other changes. To do it by hand instead, install the SDK, make the three edits in [SDK → Quick start](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#quick-start), and add your project's API key. It requires `@nestjs/core` v11.1.4 or later, and - if your application uses GraphQL - `@nestjs/graphql` v13.4.4 or later, since earlier versions of either package lack the hooks the SDK needs for proper instrumentation.

Instrumentation isn't limited to REST: `http`, `rpc`, and `grpc` are each covered and configured the same way in `ObserveModule.forRoot()`, and queue consumers and cron jobs are covered by the SDK's job instrumentation - they get their own [Jobs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#jobs) view, with queue wait time and retry attempts alongside the usual duration and failure rate. A request that fans out from your API into another HTTP or RPC service still resolves to one [distributed trace](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md), once that downstream service is set up to pick up the propagated trace id - see [SDK → Propagating trace ids between services](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#propagating-trace-ids-between-services). Queue jobs need nothing extra: one added from inside a traced request carries that request's trace id to the worker that runs it (SDK 0.3.0 or later on both sides), while repeatable jobs, `@nestjs/schedule` handlers and jobs added outside any request start their own trace.

## What's an Observability Event?

Usage is metered in **Observability Events (OEs)** - one per request, background job run, error, log entry, or trace span your applications report. Each plan includes a monthly allowance of OEs, and what happens beyond it depends on the plan: **Free** keeps recording requests, jobs and errors past its 300k events, with most traces arriving without their spans, and refuses new telemetry at twice the allowance until the next billing period; **Pro** and **Scale** allow overage instead of a hard stop, billed per extra million events, so a busy month doesn't mean lost data; [spike protection](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#spike-protection) pauses overage when usage surges, server errors still collected, and an optional [monthly overage budget](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#monthly-overage-budget) caps what it can cost. Free also pauses most waterfalls for the rest of any UTC day that passes 30k events, so one noisy day can't spend the month - see [Free plan limits](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#free-plan-limits). Set **quota notifications** on the [Usage](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#usage) page (up to five thresholds, e.g. 50%/80%/100%) to get an email before you find out from the invoice. See [Billing & usage](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md) for the full pricing table.

## Can I reduce telemetry volume?

Yes - [spend controls](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#spend-controls), configured per project on **Billing → Spend controls**: sample spans on a noisy project, cap ingestion with a rate limit, or drop known-noisy traffic like health checks, all with no redeploy. Sampling and drop filters never remove errors, since they're low-volume and exactly what you want when something breaks. A rate cap is a circuit breaker rather than a filter - once it engages, everything above it is refused, errors included - so set it well above your normal peak. [Cost attribution](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#cost-attribution) tells you which routes and jobs are worth targeting before you set one up.

## Why is my Spans page empty when Usage shows spans?

Because they count different things. Every request your application serves records a whole tree of **auto-instrumented** spans - the controller, each service and repository call - and each one is a separate [Observability Event](#whats-an-observability-event) under **Spans** on the Usage page. Database queries and outbound HTTP calls show up in the same tree but [aren't billed](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#database-queries-and-outbound-http). That's normally the largest slice of a project's volume. The [Spans](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/telemetry.md#spans) analytics page lists only the **custom** spans you named yourself with [`TracerService.createSpan()`](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#creating-spans), so an application that never calls it has a busy Spans figure in Usage and an empty Spans page. The auto-instrumented ones are read per trace, in the [waterfall](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#reading-the-waterfall) on any request's detail page. To reduce the volume, turn on [span sampling](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/billing.md#spend-controls) - it's trace-coherent, so sampled traces keep complete waterfalls.

## How long is my telemetry retained?

Retention is set by plan: 3 days on Free, 30 days on Pro, 90 days on Scale, and a negotiated period on Enterprise. Data older than your plan's window is deleted automatically. This is also the ceiling for other time-based features - an [SLO](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/slos.md#retention-is-the-ceiling)'s compliance window, for instance, can't exceed how long your plan keeps the underlying data.

One exception, in the other direction: **trace spans are kept for 7 days rather than the full window when the execution was both fast and successful** - under 1 second, no 5xx, no failed job. Slow and failing executions keep their spans for the full window, and every execution keeps its own record either way. See [Traces → How long waterfalls are kept](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/traces.md#how-long-waterfalls-are-kept).

## What if I cancel or downgrade?

If you cancel, your applications keep running and sending telemetry as normal, but you lose access to the dashboard once the subscription ends. If you downgrade to a plan with shorter retention, older data may expire sooner than it otherwise would - downgrading doesn't delete anything immediately, it just shortens how long new and existing data is kept going forward.

## Is my data redacted or identifiable?

Only what you choose to send, in both cases. When log forwarding (`forwardLogs`) is on, redaction is on by default the same moment it is - built-in patterns catch bearer tokens, JWTs, AWS key ids, PEM private keys, `key=value` secrets, and Luhn-valid card numbers, and you can add your own patterns or attribute-key names on top. Log forwarding itself is a Pro-and-above feature; see [SDK → Logs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/sdk.md#logs).

For users, `getUserId` reports whatever identifier your app already uses for a person - a user id, an account id, a tenant-scoped id - and the dashboard treats it as an opaque string; it's never resolved into a name, email, or anything else. Reporting a user identifier at all is optional, and it's recommended you use an internal id rather than anything personally identifying. See [Users](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/users.md#reporting-a-user).

## Alerts vs. SLOs vs. Issues?

**Alerts** watch a metric and notify you the moment it crosses a threshold or deviates from its own baseline. **SLOs** are a longer-horizon view on top of the same telemetry - "99.9% of requests under 300ms over 28 days" - with an error budget and burn rate instead of a single reading; a burn-rate alert is just a regular alert rule pointed at an SLO. **Issues** are where the resulting work gets tracked - create one by hand, or have a firing alert open one automatically, pre-filled with severity and a link back to the telemetry that triggered it. See [Alerts](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md), [SLOs](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/slos.md), and [Issues](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/issues.md).

## Can I get notified if my app goes silent?

Yes, that's **absence detection**: a **Telemetry silence** rule fires once an application has gone quiet longer than a tolerance you set (2 minutes to 7 days), using the same runtime heartbeat the Profiler samples. A **Job silence** rule does the same for one named job, or for any job in the project if left unscoped. Neither fires on a scope that has never reported anything - "not yet integrated" isn't treated as "down." See [Alerts → Absence detection](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/alerts.md#absence-detection).

## Does it support SSO and access roles?

SSO is available on Scale and Enterprise - configure a connection under **Teams → SSO**, verify the domains that should route through it, and enforcement only takes effect once you explicitly switch it on. Independently of SSO, every project member has one of three access levels - Read, Write, or Admin - controlling whether they can view telemetry, make changes, or manage members, settings, and billing. See [Applications → Single sign-on](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/applications.md#single-sign-on) and [Overview → Access control](https://www.observe.nestjs.com/llms/overview.md#access-control).

## Why not self-host OpenTelemetry?

Auto-instrumentation, tracing, error monitoring, logs, and alerting come out of the box, so you don't need to stand up and operate your own collectors, storage, and dashboards to get the same visibility - and the instrumentation itself is written around Nest's request lifecycle rather than a generic setup you'd have to configure by hand.
